case_info.scenario: A woman in her 50s was referred to our dermatology clinic due to a nodular lesion on her left cheek (Figure 1A). The lesion had been present for more than 5 years, with progressive slow growth. On examination, it measured 2.5 cm in diameter, was firm to palpation—lacking the typical consistency of a cyst or a lipoma—was nonmobile and apparently adherent to underlying structures, was asymptomatic with no reported pain or discomfort, and extended into the oral cavity. No additional lesions were observed on the head or neck. The patient had no relevant medical history and denied any prior facial injections. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined, hypervascular, solid tumor located within the subcutaneous tissue, measuring 2.1 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. A biopsy of the central portion of the lesion was performed (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A. Clinical image of a well-demarcated, nodular lesion (arrowhead) measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter located on the left cheek and protruding into the oral cavity. B. Immunohistochemistry showing spindle-cell neoplasm located within the subcutaneous tissue, composed of medium-sized, basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern within a fibrous stroma containing thin-walled blood vessels, including larger branching staghorn vessels (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The biopsy revealed a neoplastic proliferation of medium-sized, spindle-shaped basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern on a fibrous stroma with small-caliber blood vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34, factor XIIIa, and STAT6. Given the histological findings and CD34 positivity, RNA sequencing was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue to detect sarcoma-associated gene fusions. The analysis revealed theNAB2::STAT6fusion, which confirmed the final diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). A full staging workup showed no lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease. Moreover, given that the tumor measured 2.5 cm in diameter, its mitotic count assessed over 10 high-power fields was 0, it exhibited less than 10% necrosis, and occurred in a patient in her 50s, it scores only 1 point on the risk of metastasis model for SFTs by Demicco et al.1The lesion was subsequently removed with wide surgical margins, with no recurrence 8 months after surgery. SFT is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm—with an estimated annual incidence of 0.35 per 100 000 individuals—first described in the pleura but now known to occur in various anatomical sites, including the abdominal cavity, orbit, retroperitoneum, and, less frequently, the skin.1-5Historically, hemangiopericytoma was considered a distinct entity, but molecular, immunohistochemical, and morphological studies have demonstrated that hemangiopericytomas and SFTs lie along the same tumor spectrum. They most commonly present as a slowly enlarging, painless mass that may produce different local mass effects depending on its location; pleural lesions may also cause cough or dyspnea. In cutaneous presentations, SFT arises from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue.2,3 The largest case series of cutaneous SFTs to date described a female predominance and preferential location on the head and neck, followed by the thigh and back, with a median age of 46.5 years at diagnosis.2Histologically, SFTs are composed of spindle cells arranged in a patternless architecture, often with alternating areas of hypocellularity and hypercellularity, variably collagenous stroma, and hemangiopericytomalike vessels. Variants such as lipomatous, fascicular, and storiform patterns have been reported.2-4 Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for CD34, Bcl-2, and CD99, although expression can be variable. Nuclear expression of STAT6, due to theNAB2::STAT6gene fusion, has emerged as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic marker.4,6Molecular confirmation via detection of this fusion gene provides additional diagnostic certainty.2-4,6 Differentiating SFT from other CD34-positive spindle-cell neoplasms can be difficult. Historically, many cases were misdiagnosed prior to the identification of theNAB2::STAT6fusion.2-4Fat-free or low-fat spindle-cell lipomas pose one of the most challenging differential diagnoses due to similar morphology and CD34 expression. However, spindle-cell lipomas typically display a school of fish arrangement, thicker collagen bundles, and loss of retinoblastoma protein expression.2-4 Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans must also be considered, particularly when the lesion is dermally based. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans exhibit a uniform storiform pattern and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern—features absent in SFT—and are characterized by the specificCOL1A1::PDGFBgene fusion.2,3Superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors, while also expressing CD34, generally show greater cytologic atypia and focal cytokeratin positivity.2 The metastatic potential of SFTs can be stratified using the Demicco risk assessment model, which incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis.1Additionally, telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter andTP53variants have been associated with more aggressive clinical behavior.7,8 Management of cutaneous SFTs is challenging due to their unpredictable biological behavior; between 10% and 25% of SFTs recur, and 10-year survival rates range from 73% to 100%, even in tumors initially classified histologically as low risk.2,3Complete wide local excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs micrographic surgery has also been proposed to ensure clear margins, minimize recurrence, and preserve tissue—particularly in cosmetically sensitive areas.5 This case underscores the importance of recognizing the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of cutaneous SFTs. Awareness of theNAB2::STAT6translocation is essential for accurate diagnosis, which in turn informs appropriate treatment and long-term follow-up.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 50s was referred to our dermatology clinic due to a nodular lesion on her left cheek (Figure 1A). The lesion had been present for more than 5 years, with progressive slow growth. On examination, it measured 2.5 cm in diameter, was firm to palpation—lacking the typical consistency of a cyst or a lipoma—was nonmobile and apparently adherent to underlying structures, was asymptomatic with no reported pain or discomfort, and extended into the oral cavity. No additional lesions were observed on the head or neck. The patient had no relevant medical history and denied any prior facial injections. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined, hypervascular, solid tumor located within the subcutaneous tissue, measuring 2.1 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. A biopsy of the central portion of the lesion was performed (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A. Clinical image of a well-demarcated, nodular lesion (arrowhead) measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter located on the left cheek and protruding into the oral cavity. B. Immunohistochemistry showing spindle-cell neoplasm located within the subcutaneous tissue, composed of medium-sized, basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern within a fibrous stroma containing thin-walled blood vessels, including larger branching staghorn vessels (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The biopsy revealed a neoplastic proliferation of medium-sized, spindle-shaped basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern on a fibrous stroma with small-caliber blood vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34, factor XIIIa, and STAT6. Given the histological findings and CD34 positivity, RNA sequencing was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue to detect sarcoma-associated gene fusions. The analysis revealed theNAB2::STAT6fusion, which confirmed the final diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). A full staging workup showed no lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease. Moreover, given that the tumor measured 2.5 cm in diameter, its mitotic count assessed over 10 high-power fields was 0, it exhibited less than 10% necrosis, and occurred in a patient in her 50s, it scores only 1 point on the risk of metastasis model for SFTs by Demicco et al.1The lesion was subsequently removed with wide surgical margins, with no recurrence 8 months after surgery. SFT is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm—with an estimated annual incidence of 0.35 per 100 000 individuals—first described in the pleura but now known to occur in various anatomical sites, including the abdominal cavity, orbit, retroperitoneum, and, less frequently, the skin.1-5Historically, hemangiopericytoma was considered a distinct entity, but molecular, immunohistochemical, and morphological studies have demonstrated that hemangiopericytomas and SFTs lie along the same tumor spectrum. They most commonly present as a slowly enlarging, painless mass that may produce different local mass effects depending on its location; pleural lesions may also cause cough or dyspnea. In cutaneous presentations, SFT arises from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue.2,3 The largest case series of cutaneous SFTs to date described a female predominance and preferential location on the head and neck, followed by the thigh and back, with a median age of 46.5 years at diagnosis.2Histologically, SFTs are composed of spindle cells arranged in a patternless architecture, often with alternating areas of hypocellularity and hypercellularity, variably collagenous stroma, and hemangiopericytomalike vessels. Variants such as lipomatous, fascicular, and storiform patterns have been reported.2-4 Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for CD34, Bcl-2, and CD99, although expression can be variable. Nuclear expression of STAT6, due to theNAB2::STAT6gene fusion, has emerged as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic marker.4,6Molecular confirmation via detection of this fusion gene provides additional diagnostic certainty.2-4,6 Differentiating SFT from other CD34-positive spindle-cell neoplasms can be difficult. Historically, many cases were misdiagnosed prior to the identification of theNAB2::STAT6fusion.2-4Fat-free or low-fat spindle-cell lipomas pose one of the most challenging differential diagnoses due to similar morphology and CD34 expression. However, spindle-cell lipomas typically display a school of fish arrangement, thicker collagen bundles, and loss of retinoblastoma protein expression.2-4 Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans must also be considered, particularly when the lesion is dermally based. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans exhibit a uniform storiform pattern and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern—features absent in SFT—and are characterized by the specificCOL1A1::PDGFBgene fusion.2,3Superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors, while also expressing CD34, generally show greater cytologic atypia and focal cytokeratin positivity.2 The metastatic potential of SFTs can be stratified using the Demicco risk assessment model, which incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis.1Additionally, telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter andTP53variants have been associated with more aggressive clinical behavior.7,8 Management of cutaneous SFTs is challenging due to their unpredictable biological behavior; between 10% and 25% of SFTs recur, and 10-year survival rates range from 73% to 100%, even in tumors initially classified histologically as low risk.2,3Complete wide local excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs micrographic surgery has also been proposed to ensure clear margins, minimize recurrence, and preserve tissue—particularly in cosmetically sensitive areas.5 This case underscores the importance of recognizing the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of cutaneous SFTs. Awareness of theNAB2::STAT6translocation is essential for accurate diagnosis, which in turn informs appropriate treatment and long-term follow-up.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 50s was referred to our dermatology clinic due to a nodular lesion on her left cheek (Figure 1A). The lesion had been present for more than 5 years, with progressive slow growth. On examination, it measured 2.5 cm in diameter, was firm to palpation—lacking the typical consistency of a cyst or a lipoma—was nonmobile and apparently adherent to underlying structures, was asymptomatic with no reported pain or discomfort, and extended into the oral cavity. No additional lesions were observed on the head or neck. The patient had no relevant medical history and denied any prior facial injections. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined, hypervascular, solid tumor located within the subcutaneous tissue, measuring 2.1 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. A biopsy of the central portion of the lesion was performed (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A. Clinical image of a well-demarcated, nodular lesion (arrowhead) measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter located on the left cheek and protruding into the oral cavity. B. Immunohistochemistry showing spindle-cell neoplasm located within the subcutaneous tissue, composed of medium-sized, basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern within a fibrous stroma containing thin-walled blood vessels, including larger branching staghorn vessels (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The biopsy revealed a neoplastic proliferation of medium-sized, spindle-shaped basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern on a fibrous stroma with small-caliber blood vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34, factor XIIIa, and STAT6. Given the histological findings and CD34 positivity, RNA sequencing was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue to detect sarcoma-associated gene fusions. The analysis revealed theNAB2::STAT6fusion, which confirmed the final diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). A full staging workup showed no lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease. Moreover, given that the tumor measured 2.5 cm in diameter, its mitotic count assessed over 10 high-power fields was 0, it exhibited less than 10% necrosis, and occurred in a patient in her 50s, it scores only 1 point on the risk of metastasis model for SFTs by Demicco et al.1The lesion was subsequently removed with wide surgical margins, with no recurrence 8 months after surgery. SFT is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm—with an estimated annual incidence of 0.35 per 100 000 individuals—first described in the pleura but now known to occur in various anatomical sites, including the abdominal cavity, orbit, retroperitoneum, and, less frequently, the skin.1-5Historically, hemangiopericytoma was considered a distinct entity, but molecular, immunohistochemical, and morphological studies have demonstrated that hemangiopericytomas and SFTs lie along the same tumor spectrum. They most commonly present as a slowly enlarging, painless mass that may produce different local mass effects depending on its location; pleural lesions may also cause cough or dyspnea. In cutaneous presentations, SFT arises from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue.2,3 The largest case series of cutaneous SFTs to date described a female predominance and preferential location on the head and neck, followed by the thigh and back, with a median age of 46.5 years at diagnosis.2Histologically, SFTs are composed of spindle cells arranged in a patternless architecture, often with alternating areas of hypocellularity and hypercellularity, variably collagenous stroma, and hemangiopericytomalike vessels. Variants such as lipomatous, fascicular, and storiform patterns have been reported.2-4 Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for CD34, Bcl-2, and CD99, although expression can be variable. Nuclear expression of STAT6, due to theNAB2::STAT6gene fusion, has emerged as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic marker.4,6Molecular confirmation via detection of this fusion gene provides additional diagnostic certainty.2-4,6 Differentiating SFT from other CD34-positive spindle-cell neoplasms can be difficult. Historically, many cases were misdiagnosed prior to the identification of theNAB2::STAT6fusion.2-4Fat-free or low-fat spindle-cell lipomas pose one of the most challenging differential diagnoses due to similar morphology and CD34 expression. However, spindle-cell lipomas typically display a school of fish arrangement, thicker collagen bundles, and loss of retinoblastoma protein expression.2-4 Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans must also be considered, particularly when the lesion is dermally based. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans exhibit a uniform storiform pattern and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern—features absent in SFT—and are characterized by the specificCOL1A1::PDGFBgene fusion.2,3Superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors, while also expressing CD34, generally show greater cytologic atypia and focal cytokeratin positivity.2 The metastatic potential of SFTs can be stratified using the Demicco risk assessment model, which incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis.1Additionally, telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter andTP53variants have been associated with more aggressive clinical behavior.7,8 Management of cutaneous SFTs is challenging due to their unpredictable biological behavior; between 10% and 25% of SFTs recur, and 10-year survival rates range from 73% to 100%, even in tumors initially classified histologically as low risk.2,3Complete wide local excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs micrographic surgery has also been proposed to ensure clear margins, minimize recurrence, and preserve tissue—particularly in cosmetically sensitive areas.5 This case underscores the importance of recognizing the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of cutaneous SFTs. Awareness of theNAB2::STAT6translocation is essential for accurate diagnosis, which in turn informs appropriate treatment and long-term follow-up.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 50s was referred to our dermatology clinic due to a nodular lesion on her left cheek (Figure 1A). The lesion had been present for more than 5 years, with progressive slow growth. On examination, it measured 2.5 cm in diameter, was firm to palpation—lacking the typical consistency of a cyst or a lipoma—was nonmobile and apparently adherent to underlying structures, was asymptomatic with no reported pain or discomfort, and extended into the oral cavity. No additional lesions were observed on the head or neck. The patient had no relevant medical history and denied any prior facial injections. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined, hypervascular, solid tumor located within the subcutaneous tissue, measuring 2.1 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. A biopsy of the central portion of the lesion was performed (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A. Clinical image of a well-demarcated, nodular lesion (arrowhead) measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter located on the left cheek and protruding into the oral cavity. B. Immunohistochemistry showing spindle-cell neoplasm located within the subcutaneous tissue, composed of medium-sized, basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern within a fibrous stroma containing thin-walled blood vessels, including larger branching staghorn vessels (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The biopsy revealed a neoplastic proliferation of medium-sized, spindle-shaped basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern on a fibrous stroma with small-caliber blood vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34, factor XIIIa, and STAT6. Given the histological findings and CD34 positivity, RNA sequencing was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue to detect sarcoma-associated gene fusions. The analysis revealed theNAB2::STAT6fusion, which confirmed the final diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). A full staging workup showed no lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease. Moreover, given that the tumor measured 2.5 cm in diameter, its mitotic count assessed over 10 high-power fields was 0, it exhibited less than 10% necrosis, and occurred in a patient in her 50s, it scores only 1 point on the risk of metastasis model for SFTs by Demicco et al.1The lesion was subsequently removed with wide surgical margins, with no recurrence 8 months after surgery. SFT is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm—with an estimated annual incidence of 0.35 per 100 000 individuals—first described in the pleura but now known to occur in various anatomical sites, including the abdominal cavity, orbit, retroperitoneum, and, less frequently, the skin.1-5Historically, hemangiopericytoma was considered a distinct entity, but molecular, immunohistochemical, and morphological studies have demonstrated that hemangiopericytomas and SFTs lie along the same tumor spectrum. They most commonly present as a slowly enlarging, painless mass that may produce different local mass effects depending on its location; pleural lesions may also cause cough or dyspnea. In cutaneous presentations, SFT arises from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue.2,3 The largest case series of cutaneous SFTs to date described a female predominance and preferential location on the head and neck, followed by the thigh and back, with a median age of 46.5 years at diagnosis.2Histologically, SFTs are composed of spindle cells arranged in a patternless architecture, often with alternating areas of hypocellularity and hypercellularity, variably collagenous stroma, and hemangiopericytomalike vessels. Variants such as lipomatous, fascicular, and storiform patterns have been reported.2-4 Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for CD34, Bcl-2, and CD99, although expression can be variable. Nuclear expression of STAT6, due to theNAB2::STAT6gene fusion, has emerged as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic marker.4,6Molecular confirmation via detection of this fusion gene provides additional diagnostic certainty.2-4,6 Differentiating SFT from other CD34-positive spindle-cell neoplasms can be difficult. Historically, many cases were misdiagnosed prior to the identification of theNAB2::STAT6fusion.2-4Fat-free or low-fat spindle-cell lipomas pose one of the most challenging differential diagnoses due to similar morphology and CD34 expression. However, spindle-cell lipomas typically display a school of fish arrangement, thicker collagen bundles, and loss of retinoblastoma protein expression.2-4 Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans must also be considered, particularly when the lesion is dermally based. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans exhibit a uniform storiform pattern and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern—features absent in SFT—and are characterized by the specificCOL1A1::PDGFBgene fusion.2,3Superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors, while also expressing CD34, generally show greater cytologic atypia and focal cytokeratin positivity.2 The metastatic potential of SFTs can be stratified using the Demicco risk assessment model, which incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis.1Additionally, telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter andTP53variants have been associated with more aggressive clinical behavior.7,8 Management of cutaneous SFTs is challenging due to their unpredictable biological behavior; between 10% and 25% of SFTs recur, and 10-year survival rates range from 73% to 100%, even in tumors initially classified histologically as low risk.2,3Complete wide local excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs micrographic surgery has also been proposed to ensure clear margins, minimize recurrence, and preserve tissue—particularly in cosmetically sensitive areas.5 This case underscores the importance of recognizing the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of cutaneous SFTs. Awareness of theNAB2::STAT6translocation is essential for accurate diagnosis, which in turn informs appropriate treatment and long-term follow-up.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 50s was referred to our dermatology clinic due to a nodular lesion on her left cheek (Figure 1A). The lesion had been present for more than 5 years, with progressive slow growth. On examination, it measured 2.5 cm in diameter, was firm to palpation—lacking the typical consistency of a cyst or a lipoma—was nonmobile and apparently adherent to underlying structures, was asymptomatic with no reported pain or discomfort, and extended into the oral cavity. No additional lesions were observed on the head or neck. The patient had no relevant medical history and denied any prior facial injections. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined, hypervascular, solid tumor located within the subcutaneous tissue, measuring 2.1 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. A biopsy of the central portion of the lesion was performed (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A. Clinical image of a well-demarcated, nodular lesion (arrowhead) measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter located on the left cheek and protruding into the oral cavity. B. Immunohistochemistry showing spindle-cell neoplasm located within the subcutaneous tissue, composed of medium-sized, basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern within a fibrous stroma containing thin-walled blood vessels, including larger branching staghorn vessels (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The biopsy revealed a neoplastic proliferation of medium-sized, spindle-shaped basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern on a fibrous stroma with small-caliber blood vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34, factor XIIIa, and STAT6. Given the histological findings and CD34 positivity, RNA sequencing was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue to detect sarcoma-associated gene fusions. The analysis revealed theNAB2::STAT6fusion, which confirmed the final diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). A full staging workup showed no lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease. Moreover, given that the tumor measured 2.5 cm in diameter, its mitotic count assessed over 10 high-power fields was 0, it exhibited less than 10% necrosis, and occurred in a patient in her 50s, it scores only 1 point on the risk of metastasis model for SFTs by Demicco et al.1The lesion was subsequently removed with wide surgical margins, with no recurrence 8 months after surgery. SFT is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm—with an estimated annual incidence of 0.35 per 100 000 individuals—first described in the pleura but now known to occur in various anatomical sites, including the abdominal cavity, orbit, retroperitoneum, and, less frequently, the skin.1-5Historically, hemangiopericytoma was considered a distinct entity, but molecular, immunohistochemical, and morphological studies have demonstrated that hemangiopericytomas and SFTs lie along the same tumor spectrum. They most commonly present as a slowly enlarging, painless mass that may produce different local mass effects depending on its location; pleural lesions may also cause cough or dyspnea. In cutaneous presentations, SFT arises from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue.2,3 The largest case series of cutaneous SFTs to date described a female predominance and preferential location on the head and neck, followed by the thigh and back, with a median age of 46.5 years at diagnosis.2Histologically, SFTs are composed of spindle cells arranged in a patternless architecture, often with alternating areas of hypocellularity and hypercellularity, variably collagenous stroma, and hemangiopericytomalike vessels. Variants such as lipomatous, fascicular, and storiform patterns have been reported.2-4 Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for CD34, Bcl-2, and CD99, although expression can be variable. Nuclear expression of STAT6, due to theNAB2::STAT6gene fusion, has emerged as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic marker.4,6Molecular confirmation via detection of this fusion gene provides additional diagnostic certainty.2-4,6 Differentiating SFT from other CD34-positive spindle-cell neoplasms can be difficult. Historically, many cases were misdiagnosed prior to the identification of theNAB2::STAT6fusion.2-4Fat-free or low-fat spindle-cell lipomas pose one of the most challenging differential diagnoses due to similar morphology and CD34 expression. However, spindle-cell lipomas typically display a school of fish arrangement, thicker collagen bundles, and loss of retinoblastoma protein expression.2-4 Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans must also be considered, particularly when the lesion is dermally based. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans exhibit a uniform storiform pattern and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern—features absent in SFT—and are characterized by the specificCOL1A1::PDGFBgene fusion.2,3Superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors, while also expressing CD34, generally show greater cytologic atypia and focal cytokeratin positivity.2 The metastatic potential of SFTs can be stratified using the Demicco risk assessment model, which incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis.1Additionally, telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter andTP53variants have been associated with more aggressive clinical behavior.7,8 Management of cutaneous SFTs is challenging due to their unpredictable biological behavior; between 10% and 25% of SFTs recur, and 10-year survival rates range from 73% to 100%, even in tumors initially classified histologically as low risk.2,3Complete wide local excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs micrographic surgery has also been proposed to ensure clear margins, minimize recurrence, and preserve tissue—particularly in cosmetically sensitive areas.5 This case underscores the importance of recognizing the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of cutaneous SFTs. Awareness of theNAB2::STAT6translocation is essential for accurate diagnosis, which in turn informs appropriate treatment and long-term follow-up.

The analysis revealed theNAB2::STAT6fusion, which confirmed the final diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). A full staging workup showed no lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease. Moreover, given that the tumor measured 2.5 cm in diameter, its mitotic count assessed over 10 high-power fields was 0, it exhibited less than 10% necrosis, and occurred in a patient in her 50s, it scores only 1 point on the risk of metastasis model for SFTs by Demicco et al.1The lesion was subsequently removed with wide surgical margins, with no recurrence 8 months after surgery. SFT is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm—with an estimated annual incidence of 0.35 per 100 000 individuals—first described in the pleura but now known to occur in various anatomical sites, including the abdominal cavity, orbit, retroperitoneum, and, less frequently, the skin.1-5Historically, hemangiopericytoma was considered a distinct entity, but molecular, immunohistochemical, and morphological studies have demonstrated that hemangiopericytomas and SFTs lie along the same tumor spectrum. They most commonly present as a slowly enlarging, painless mass that may produce different local mass effects depending on its location; pleural lesions may also cause cough or dyspnea. In cutaneous presentations, SFT arises from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue.2,3 The largest case series of cutaneous SFTs to date described a female predominance and preferential location on the head and neck, followed by the thigh and back, with a median age of 46.5 years at diagnosis.2Histologically, SFTs are composed of spindle cells arranged in a patternless architecture, often with alternating areas of hypocellularity and hypercellularity, variably collagenous stroma, and hemangiopericytomalike vessels. Variants such as lipomatous, fascicular, and storiform patterns have been reported.2-4 Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for CD34, Bcl-2, and CD99, although expression can be variable. Nuclear expression of STAT6, due to theNAB2::STAT6gene fusion, has emerged as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic marker.4,6Molecular confirmation via detection of this fusion gene provides additional diagnostic certainty.2-4,6 Differentiating SFT from other CD34-positive spindle-cell neoplasms can be difficult. Historically, many cases were misdiagnosed prior to the identification of theNAB2::STAT6fusion.2-4Fat-free or low-fat spindle-cell lipomas pose one of the most challenging differential diagnoses due to similar morphology and CD34 expression. However, spindle-cell lipomas typically display a school of fish arrangement, thicker collagen bundles, and loss of retinoblastoma protein expression.2-4 Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans must also be considered, particularly when the lesion is dermally based. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans exhibit a uniform storiform pattern and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern—features absent in SFT—and are characterized by the specificCOL1A1::PDGFBgene fusion.2,3Superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors, while also expressing CD34, generally show greater cytologic atypia and focal cytokeratin positivity.2 The metastatic potential of SFTs can be stratified using the Demicco risk assessment model, which incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis.1Additionally, telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter andTP53variants have been associated with more aggressive clinical behavior.7,8 Management of cutaneous SFTs is challenging due to their unpredictable biological behavior; between 10% and 25% of SFTs recur, and 10-year survival rates range from 73% to 100%, even in tumors initially classified histologically as low risk.2,3Complete wide local excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs micrographic surgery has also been proposed to ensure clear margins, minimize recurrence, and preserve tissue—particularly in cosmetically sensitive areas.5 This case underscores the importance of recognizing the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of cutaneous SFTs. Awareness of theNAB2::STAT6translocation is essential for accurate diagnosis, which in turn informs appropriate treatment and long-term follow-up.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."

       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 50s was referred to our dermatology clinic due to a nodular lesion on her left cheek (Figure 1A). The lesion had been present for more than 5 years, with progressive slow growth. On examination, it measured 2.5 cm in diameter, was firm to palpation—lacking the typical consistency of a cyst or a lipoma—was nonmobile and apparently adherent to underlying structures, was asymptomatic with no reported pain or discomfort, and extended into the oral cavity. No additional lesions were observed on the head or neck. The patient had no relevant medical history and denied any prior facial injections. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined, hypervascular, solid tumor located within the subcutaneous tissue, measuring 2.1 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. A biopsy of the central portion of the lesion was performed (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A. Clinical image of a well-demarcated, nodular lesion (arrowhead) measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter located on the left cheek and protruding into the oral cavity. B. Immunohistochemistry showing spindle-cell neoplasm located within the subcutaneous tissue, composed of medium-sized, basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern within a fibrous stroma containing thin-walled blood vessels, including larger branching staghorn vessels (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The biopsy revealed a neoplastic proliferation of medium-sized, spindle-shaped basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern on a fibrous stroma with small-caliber blood vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34, factor XIIIa, and STAT6. Given the histological findings and CD34 positivity, RNA sequencing was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue to detect sarcoma-associated gene fusions. The analysis revealed theNAB2::STAT6fusion, which confirmed the final diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). A full staging workup showed no lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease. Moreover, given that the tumor measured 2.5 cm in diameter, its mitotic count assessed over 10 high-power fields was 0, it exhibited less than 10% necrosis, and occurred in a patient in her 50s, it scores only 1 point on the risk of metastasis model for SFTs by Demicco et al.1The lesion was subsequently removed with wide surgical margins, with no recurrence 8 months after surgery. SFT is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm—with an estimated annual incidence of 0.35 per 100 000 individuals—first described in the pleura but now known to occur in various anatomical sites, including the abdominal cavity, orbit, retroperitoneum, and, less frequently, the skin.1-5Historically, hemangiopericytoma was considered a distinct entity, but molecular, immunohistochemical, and morphological studies have demonstrated that hemangiopericytomas and SFTs lie along the same tumor spectrum. They most commonly present as a slowly enlarging, painless mass that may produce different local mass effects depending on its location; pleural lesions may also cause cough or dyspnea. In cutaneous presentations, SFT arises from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue.2,3 The largest case series of cutaneous SFTs to date described a female predominance and preferential location on the head and neck, followed by the thigh and back, with a median age of 46.5 years at diagnosis.2Histologically, SFTs are composed of spindle cells arranged in a patternless architecture, often with alternating areas of hypocellularity and hypercellularity, variably collagenous stroma, and hemangiopericytomalike vessels. Variants such as lipomatous, fascicular, and storiform patterns have been reported.2-4 Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for CD34, Bcl-2, and CD99, although expression can be variable. Nuclear expression of STAT6, due to theNAB2::STAT6gene fusion, has emerged as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic marker.4,6Molecular confirmation via detection of this fusion gene provides additional diagnostic certainty.2-4,6 Differentiating SFT from other CD34-positive spindle-cell neoplasms can be difficult. Historically, many cases were misdiagnosed prior to the identification of theNAB2::STAT6fusion.2-4Fat-free or low-fat spindle-cell lipomas pose one of the most challenging differential diagnoses due to similar morphology and CD34 expression. However, spindle-cell lipomas typically display a school of fish arrangement, thicker collagen bundles, and loss of retinoblastoma protein expression.2-4 Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans must also be considered, particularly when the lesion is dermally based. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans exhibit a uniform storiform pattern and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern—features absent in SFT—and are characterized by the specificCOL1A1::PDGFBgene fusion.2,3Superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors, while also expressing CD34, generally show greater cytologic atypia and focal cytokeratin positivity.2 The metastatic potential of SFTs can be stratified using the Demicco risk assessment model, which incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis.1Additionally, telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter andTP53variants have been associated with more aggressive clinical behavior.7,8 Management of cutaneous SFTs is challenging due to their unpredictable biological behavior; between 10% and 25% of SFTs recur, and 10-year survival rates range from 73% to 100%, even in tumors initially classified histologically as low risk.2,3Complete wide local excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs micrographic surgery has also been proposed to ensure clear margins, minimize recurrence, and preserve tissue—particularly in cosmetically sensitive areas.5 This case underscores the importance of recognizing the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of cutaneous SFTs. Awareness of theNAB2::STAT6translocation is essential for accurate diagnosis, which in turn informs appropriate treatment and long-term follow-up.

            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.

            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop

1. Mental Demand

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

case_info.scenario: A woman in her 50s was referred to our dermatology clinic due to a nodular lesion on her left cheek (Figure 1A). The lesion had been present for more than 5 years, with progressive slow growth. On examination, it measured 2.5 cm in diameter, was firm to palpation—lacking the typical consistency of a cyst or a lipoma—was nonmobile and apparently adherent to underlying structures, was asymptomatic with no reported pain or discomfort, and extended into the oral cavity. No additional lesions were observed on the head or neck. The patient had no relevant medical history and denied any prior facial injections. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed a well-defined, hypervascular, solid tumor located within the subcutaneous tissue, measuring 2.1 × 2.5 × 2.3 cm, with no evidence of invasion into adjacent structures. A biopsy of the central portion of the lesion was performed (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A. Clinical image of a well-demarcated, nodular lesion (arrowhead) measuring approximately 2.5 cm in diameter located on the left cheek and protruding into the oral cavity. B. Immunohistochemistry showing spindle-cell neoplasm located within the subcutaneous tissue, composed of medium-sized, basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern within a fibrous stroma containing thin-walled blood vessels, including larger branching staghorn vessels (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×10).
case_info.explanation: The biopsy revealed a neoplastic proliferation of medium-sized, spindle-shaped basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, arranged in a sheetlike pattern on a fibrous stroma with small-caliber blood vessels (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for CD34, factor XIIIa, and STAT6. Given the histological findings and CD34 positivity, RNA sequencing was performed on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded tissue to detect sarcoma-associated gene fusions. The analysis revealed theNAB2::STAT6fusion, which confirmed the final diagnosis of solitary fibrous tumor (SFT). A full staging workup showed no lymphadenopathy or metastatic disease. Moreover, given that the tumor measured 2.5 cm in diameter, its mitotic count assessed over 10 high-power fields was 0, it exhibited less than 10% necrosis, and occurred in a patient in her 50s, it scores only 1 point on the risk of metastasis model for SFTs by Demicco et al.1The lesion was subsequently removed with wide surgical margins, with no recurrence 8 months after surgery. SFT is a rare mesenchymal neoplasm—with an estimated annual incidence of 0.35 per 100 000 individuals—first described in the pleura but now known to occur in various anatomical sites, including the abdominal cavity, orbit, retroperitoneum, and, less frequently, the skin.1-5Historically, hemangiopericytoma was considered a distinct entity, but molecular, immunohistochemical, and morphological studies have demonstrated that hemangiopericytomas and SFTs lie along the same tumor spectrum. They most commonly present as a slowly enlarging, painless mass that may produce different local mass effects depending on its location; pleural lesions may also cause cough or dyspnea. In cutaneous presentations, SFT arises from the dermis or subcutaneous tissue.2,3 The largest case series of cutaneous SFTs to date described a female predominance and preferential location on the head and neck, followed by the thigh and back, with a median age of 46.5 years at diagnosis.2Histologically, SFTs are composed of spindle cells arranged in a patternless architecture, often with alternating areas of hypocellularity and hypercellularity, variably collagenous stroma, and hemangiopericytomalike vessels. Variants such as lipomatous, fascicular, and storiform patterns have been reported.2-4 Immunohistochemical staining typically shows positivity for CD34, Bcl-2, and CD99, although expression can be variable. Nuclear expression of STAT6, due to theNAB2::STAT6gene fusion, has emerged as a highly specific and sensitive diagnostic marker.4,6Molecular confirmation via detection of this fusion gene provides additional diagnostic certainty.2-4,6 Differentiating SFT from other CD34-positive spindle-cell neoplasms can be difficult. Historically, many cases were misdiagnosed prior to the identification of theNAB2::STAT6fusion.2-4Fat-free or low-fat spindle-cell lipomas pose one of the most challenging differential diagnoses due to similar morphology and CD34 expression. However, spindle-cell lipomas typically display a school of fish arrangement, thicker collagen bundles, and loss of retinoblastoma protein expression.2-4 Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans must also be considered, particularly when the lesion is dermally based. Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans exhibit a uniform storiform pattern and infiltrate subcutaneous fat in a honeycomb pattern—features absent in SFT—and are characterized by the specificCOL1A1::PDGFBgene fusion.2,3Superficial CD34-positive fibroblastic tumors, while also expressing CD34, generally show greater cytologic atypia and focal cytokeratin positivity.2 The metastatic potential of SFTs can be stratified using the Demicco risk assessment model, which incorporates patient age, tumor size, mitotic rate, and necrosis.1Additionally, telomerase reverse transcriptase promoter andTP53variants have been associated with more aggressive clinical behavior.7,8 Management of cutaneous SFTs is challenging due to their unpredictable biological behavior; between 10% and 25% of SFTs recur, and 10-year survival rates range from 73% to 100%, even in tumors initially classified histologically as low risk.2,3Complete wide local excision is the treatment of choice. Mohs micrographic surgery has also been proposed to ensure clear margins, minimize recurrence, and preserve tissue—particularly in cosmetically sensitive areas.5 This case underscores the importance of recognizing the clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical features of cutaneous SFTs. Awareness of theNAB2::STAT6translocation is essential for accurate diagnosis, which in turn informs appropriate treatment and long-term follow-up.
